notes:
Here is the verse-by-verse commentary for **2 Samuel 16**, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## 2 Samuel 16 – Overview

The chapter falls into four sections: David deceived by Ziba (vv. 1–4), David cursed by Shimei (vv. 5–14), Hushai insinuating himself into Absalom's court (vv. 15–19), and Ahithophel’s counsel leading Absalom to defile David's concubines (vv. 20–23). The central theological themes are David's humility under divine chastisement, the sovereignty of God over even hostile circumstances, and how human bitterness and ambition work themselves out against the backdrop of God's purposes.

---

## v. 1 — Ziba meets David with provisions

David has just passed "a little beyond the summit" — the top of the Mount of Olives (cf. 2 Sam 15:30, 32). Ziba, the servant (steward) of Mephibosheth (Saul's grandson, Jonathan's son), meets him with a generous gift: saddled donkeys, 200 loaves of bread, 100 clusters of raisins, 100 summer fruits (possibly pumpkins, cucumbers, or watermelons), and a skin of wine.

**Ellicott** notes that Ziba's later exposure (2 Sam 19:24–30) proves he "grossly slandered his master" for personal gain — yet David was in a state to believe any story of ingratitude and was deeply affected by Ziba's large contribution to his necessities. Ziba showed an "entire want of principle" and could have adhered to David's cause only because he shrewdly foresaw its ultimate success.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Precept Austin** observes: "Ziba presents a generous gift to David with food (from Mephibosheth's farm!), but a good beginning does not make for a good ending… Ziba is buttering up the king to gain what he covets." Thomas Scott is quoted: "Selfish men are often very generous in giving away the property of others for their own advantage."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

**Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic)**: "This was a generous and helpful gift from Ziba," but this good start masks ulterior motives.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

---

## v. 2 — Ziba explains the gifts

David asks, "Why do you have these?" Ziba replies that the donkeys are for the king's household to ride, the bread and fruit for the young men, and the wine for the faint.

**Precept Austin** notes the TSK comment that this reflects the Eastern mode of speech when presenting to a great man — it is for the sovereign, though phrased as "for the slaves of the servants of your majesty."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

**Matthew Henry** commends the wine being "for those that were faint, not for the king's own drinking" as a mark of discretion: "Blessed art thou, O land! when thy princes use wine for strength, as David did, and not for drunkenness, as Absalom did" (cf. Eccl. 10:17).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_samuel/16.htm

---

## vv. 3–4 — Ziba's false accusation and David's rash judgment

David asks, "Where is your master's grandson?" (Mephibosheth). Ziba falsely claims Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem, hoping "the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather." David, acting on this lie without investigation, transfers all Mephibosheth's property to Ziba. Ziba bows with feigned gratitude.

**Enduring Word**: Ziba's report was a lie, exposed in 2 Sam 19:24–30. "Ziba is an example of someone who wickedly uses a crisis for his own benefit." Morgan is quoted: Ziba "was utterly despicable, and the more so because at the moment the sorrow he brought to the heart of David was his feeling that his kindness toward Mephibosheth was ill requited." Trapp calls it "a shameless and senseless slander, uttered by a false and faithless sycophant."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Grant's Commentary**: David "ought to have immediately suspected that there was something questionable in Ziba's words." Mephibosheth's previous loyalty, plus the absurdity of a lame man expecting a kingdom while Absalom was the popular rebel, should have alerted David. "David was so deceived… that he judged the matter without inquiry. This was an unjust judgment."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-samuel-16.html

**Dr. Constable (Evangelical/Dallas)**: David "accepted Ziba's report too quickly without getting all the facts, perhaps because Ziba showed himself to be a friend of David by sustaining him in his flight. We sometimes accept a friend's analysis of the motives of another person too quickly because we do not bother to get all the facts. Here David slipped because he too willingly accepted the complimentary words of a friend."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-16.html

**Ellicott**: Ziba's story was "almost too improbable to be believed" since "a helpless cripple of the house of Saul could hardly have hoped that Absalom's rebellion would bring the throne to him." Yet David "apt to be hasty in his judgments, was in a state to believe in any story of ingratitude."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

---

## vv. 5–6 — Shimei curses and stones David

As David approaches Bahurim (a Benjamite village), Shimei son of Gera, "a man from the family of the house of Saul," comes out cursing continuously, throwing stones at David and all his servants, though the mighty men flank David on both sides.

**Enduring Word**: Shimei was a distant relative of Saul who "still resented David for replacing the dynasty of Saul." He "wanted to destroy any shred of dignity or confidence that David had left." Spurgeon is quoted: "It is very hard to bear a cowardly attack… Only the coward strikes a man when he is down."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: The road "appears to have led along the side of a narrow ravine, on the opposite side of which Shimei kept along with the fugitives, out of reach, and yet easily heard, and able to annoy them with stones." Many Benjamites "naturally felt aggrieved when the royal house passed away from their tribe" and were "ever ready to show their opposition when opportunity offered."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Mattoon (cited by Precept Austin)**: In cursing David, Shimei violates Exodus 22:28 ("You shall not curse… a ruler of your people") and invites judgment under Genesis 12:3 (the Abrahamic curse).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

---

## vv. 7–8 — Shimei's accusation: "man of bloodshed"

Shimei shouts, "Get out, get out, you worthless man of bloodshed! The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul… the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom."

**Enduring Word**: Shimei was wrong on multiple counts: David treated Saul's house with kindness; David was a man of war but not "bloodthirsty"; Saul himself brought his house to ruin. Yet "Shimei was right that the LORD had brought this upon David, but not for any of the reasons Shimei thought."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: "It is doubtful whether by 'thou bloody man' Shimei meant anything more than that he considered David responsible for 'the blood of the house of Saul'… especially in the case of Ishbosheth and of Abner, and the execution of Saul's seven descendants." Yet he "may have known of the crime in regard to Uriah."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Dr. Constable**: "Shimei's charge that David was a man of bloodshed was true; David had murdered Uriah. However, Shimei meant David was responsible for the murders of Abner and Ish-bosheth, which was not true."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-16.html

**Precept Austin** (via Swindoll): "Shimei was your basic reprobate — the kind of person who kicks you while you're on your face, down and out."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

---

## vv. 9–10 — Abishai's anger and David's restraint

Abishai (son of Zeruiah, David's nephew) calls Shimei a "dead dog" and asks permission to cut off his head. David rebukes him: "What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah? If he curses me because the LORD told him, 'Curse David,' who can ask, 'Why did you do this?'"

**Enduring Word**: David's response shows four reasons for restraint: (i) David was not a bloodthirsty man — ironically, if he were what Shimei claimed, Shimei would be dead; (ii) David saw God's hand in every circumstance ("the LORD has said to him"); (iii) David kept perspective — his real problem was Absalom, not Shimei; (iv) David trusted God with the future.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Gill (Baptist/older)**: "Not by way of command, or a precept of his; for to curse the ruler of the people is contrary to the word and law of God… nor by any operation of his spirit moving and exciting him to it… but by the secret providence of God ordering, directing, and overruling all circumstances."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/16.htm

**Ellicott**: "David, throughout, recognises that all his sufferings were from the Lord's hand, and he wishes to submit himself entirely to His will. He does not, of course, mean to justify Shimei's wrong; but only to say that, as far as his sin bears upon himself, it is of Divine appointment and he cannot resent it."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Dr. Constable**: "The willingness to listen to one's critics and even to one's enemies may be the only way to discover the truth of God." David succeeded where he had previously failed with Nabal (1 Sam 25). "For David to control his temper was a greater victory than slaying Goliath (Proverbs 16:32)."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-16.html

**Desiring God (Reformed Baptist – John Piper)**: In a sermon touching this passage, Piper highlights David's reply as a model of humble self-restraint when one could easily take revenge.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/man-of-war-and-grace

---

## vv. 11–12 — "Let him curse, for the LORD has told him"

David reasons: if his own son seeks his life, how much more this Benjamite? "Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today."

**Enduring Word**: David's hope that God would "repay me with good" shows he "knew that if he did what was right in the present moment, God would take care of the future." Spurgeon is quoted: "If you can revenge yourself, DON'T. If you could do it as easily as open your hand, keep it shut."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott** makes a significant textual note: The English "look on mine affliction" follows the LXX and Vulgate. The Hebrew margin has "mine eye," but the Hebrew text reads "my iniquity." Ellicott suggests "my iniquity" is "probably the true sense" — David hopes God will "mercifully look upon his sin, of which he has repented, and for which he is now bearing punishment."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Precept Austin**: "David regarded Shimei's cursing as ordained by God, with the implication that God would ultimately avenge him." The devotional note "In God's Hands" adds: "We can wait patiently until God vindicates us… You are in God's hands, no matter what others are saying about you."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

**Grant's Commentary**: "If one bows to the government of God, to leave matters in the hand of God in such cases is the way of true blessing in the end."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-samuel-16.html

---

## vv. 13–14 — Shimei continues; David rests

As they proceed, Shimei parallels them on the opposite ridge, cursing, throwing stones, and flinging dust. Finally, the king and his people arrive exhausted and "refreshed themselves there."

**Enduring Word**: "David was not without hope or comfort. God allowed comfort to find him, even if it was in the small things." In refusing to cling to the throne, David prefigures Christ (Phil. 2:6–8). Gene Edwards (A Tale of Three Kings) imagines David saying: "The throne is not mine. Not to have, not to take, not to protect, and not to keep. The throne is the LORD'S." Morgan: "This is a radiant illustration of the deep and inward peace given to any man who is living in fellowship with God in motive and desire."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: The word "weary" is "generally taken as a proper name, Ayephim, which was probably a mere caravansary" — i.e., a stopping-place.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

---

## vv. 15–16 — Absalom enters Jerusalem; Hushai greets him

Absalom and "all the men of Israel" (his followers) arrive in Jerusalem with Ahithophel. David's friend Hushai the Archite approaches Absalom crying, "Long live the king!"

**Enduring Word**: Hushai wanted to leave with David, but David sent him back to spy on Absalom and frustrate Ahithophel's counsel (2 Sam 15:32–34). Ahithophel's presence made this counter-intelligence necessary.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: The original phrase is simply "Let the king live," without direct mention of God — an example where modern English (with "God save the king") actually refers more directly to God than the ancient Hebrew.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

---

## vv. 17–19 — Hushai's clever double-speech

Absalom challenges Hushai: "Is this the loyalty you show your friend?" Hushai answers: "For the one chosen by the LORD, by the people, and by all the men of Israel — his I will be… As I served in your father's presence, so also I will serve in yours."

**Enduring Word**: "Hushai lied to Absalom, concealing his motives — like any good spy hides his or her true intentions."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Dr. Constable**: Hushai's words were "masterful double entendre." He was "really serving David in the presence of his son Absalom." Baldwin is quoted: "Hushai has kept his integrity, Absalom has been blinded by his own egoism, and the reader is permitted to see one example of the outworking of God's providence."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-16.html

**Grant's Commentary**: Hushai's answer, "not at all being a lie, was yet a masterpiece of deception." He spoke in such a way that Absalom thought Hushai meant him, but Hushai meant David. "Even in Absalom's presence he would still be serving David."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-samuel-16.html

**Gill**: Hushai "speaks very ambiguously; for this circumlocution… better agrees with David, whom he might bear in mind, than with Absalom; for the Lord had chosen David… but as for Absalom, it was only a part of them that had declared for him."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/16.htm

---

## vv. 20–21 — Ahithophel's counsel: take the concubines

Absalom asks Ahithophel for counsel. Ahithophel advises him to sleep with David's concubines, whom David left to keep the palace. This would make Absalom "a stench" to his father and would "strengthen the hands" of his followers by making reconciliation impossible.

**Enduring Word**: Ahithophel's radical advice made sense from self-interest — he had the most to lose if Absalom failed or if father and son reconciled. The counsel was also motivated by bitterness: Bathsheba was Ahithophel's granddaughter (through Eliam, 2 Sam 11:3; 23:34). "Ahithophel was willing to see these women abused, Absalom grievously sin, and the kingdom of Israel suffer greatly — all simply to satisfy his bitter longing for revenge."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: "The taking of the harem of his predecessor by the incoming monarch was an Oriental custom, to the enormity of which the mind was blunted by the practice of polygamy." The counsel made the breach "absolute and irreconcilable."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Matthew Henry**: "This was Ahithophel's cursed policy, which bespoke him rather an oracle of devil than of God." He notes that it assured Israel that Absalom "was in good earnest" and "was resolved never to make peace with his father."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_samuel/16.htm

---

## v. 22 — The act on the rooftop

A tent is pitched on the palace roof, and Absalom sleeps with his father's concubines "in the sight of all Israel."

**Enduring Word**: The location — the rooftop — is the very place where David first saw Bathsheba and began his sin (2 Sam 11:2). This fulfills Nathan's prophecy: "I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of the sun" (2 Sam 12:11–12). Clarke is quoted: "Every part of the conduct of Absalom shows him to have been a most profligate young man; he was proud, vindictive, adulterous, incestuous, a parricide, and in fine, reprobate to every good word and work."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Ellicott**: "Nathan had foretold that the nature of David's public punishment should correspond to the character of his secret crime. The fact that this punishment takes place on the very roof where David had first yielded to his guilty passion makes it particularly striking."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-16.html

**Grant's Commentary**: "Thus it was made clear that Absalom was absolutely rejecting his father. Yet what a reminder is this of God's words to David in chapter 12:11–12 that the results of David's sin would be emblazoned before the eyes of the people!"
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-samuel-16.html

---

## v. 23 — Ahithophel's reputation

"In those days the advice of Ahithophel was like the consultation of the word of God" — esteemed by both David and Absalom.

**Enduring Word**: "Ahithophel had a well-deserved reputation for giving counsel almost as good as God. But in this case, his counsel was foolish and destructive." It was foolish because motivated by bitterness; because God answered David's prayer (2 Sam 15:31) by prompting Ahithophel to give this counsel and Absalom to take it; and because "Absalom thought he could establish his kingdom through immorality."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-16/

**Desiring God (Piper)**: David's prayer "O Lord, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness" (2 Sam 15:31) is the background. Piper notes the irony: the wisest counsellor in Israel gives counsel, yet God turns hearts so that Hushai's advice is preferred (ch. 17). "Only God himself can turn the hearts like this." The "impossibility, apart from God" is the point.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-answers-better-than-we-ask

---

## Tradition-Specific Observations

**Reformed / Sovereign Grace (Desiring God, Constable, Enduring Word)**: A strong emphasis on God's sovereignty runs through all these commentaries. David's statement "the LORD has told him" is understood as David recognizing God's providential ordination of his suffering, not approving Shimei's sin. Constable notes that David was "willing to expose himself to God's word for his life and to God's judgment upon his life" — a mark of genuine repentance for Uriah's blood. Enduring Word (charismatic/Pentecostal stream) aligns closely with this, adding a Christological typology (David prefiguring Christ in Phil. 2).

**Baptist / Spurgeon (via Enduring Word)**: Spurgeon draws a pointed application: "If you can revenge yourself, DON'T. If you could do it as easily as open your hand, keep it shut. If one bitter word could end the argument, ask for grace to spare that bitter word." The emphasis is on personal holiness and restraint.

**Lutheran and Methodist sources**: No distinct Lutheran or Wesleyan commentary from the approved sites was found for this chapter in the search results. Matthew Henry (broadly Puritan/Evangelical) provides the most thorough traditional Protestant reading.

**Catholic / Orthodox**: No results were returned from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for 2 Samuel 16 verse-by-verse commentary.

**Modern scholarship (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org)**: No specific results were found in this search. The IVP Bible Background Commentary (cited by Precept Austin) notes that the Sumerian code called for an adopted son to forfeit land when he repudiated legal obligations to the adopting family — providing ANE background for David's confiscation of Mephibosheth's lands.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-16-commentary

---

**What I could not find**: Distinctive Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist, Word-of-Faith/prosperity, or hyper-grace readings of this chapter from the approved sites did not appear in search results. Likewise, the NET Bible translation notes and bibleodyssey.org pages did not return in searches for this passage.
